idea: Teach grades 6-8 in our 45-minute afterschool club to build a simple line-following robot using the Arduino kits we already own.

assessment.summary: Building a line-following robot with grades 6-8 on existing Arduino kits is a well-matched, high-value idea for this program, but two critical facts are missing: how many 45-minute sessions the unit gets, and whether the existing kits actually contain the chassis, motors, motor driver, and IR reflectance sensors a line follower requires. It cannot be authored as a single 45-minute session.

grade_level_fit.notes: Grades 6-8 stated explicitly. Middle school is a good fit for block- or C++-based Arduino work, basic circuits, and iterative sensor calibration; the concept of 'sense, decide, act' is age-appropriate.

materials_feasibility.notes: 'The Arduino kits we already own' is not specific enough. A line follower needs, beyond an Arduino board: a chassis, 2 DC gear motors + wheels, a motor driver (L298N/TB6612 or a motor shield), 2+ IR reflectance sensors (e.g. TCRT5000 or a QTR array), battery holder/pack, and a track surface (black electrical tape on white poster board). Common Uno starter kits include LEDs, servos, and jumper wires but no chassis, motor driver, or IR sensors, so a purchase may be required. Quantity per team is also unstated.

instructor_capability.notes: Teachable by a non-specialist with prep: the wiring is solderless breadboard/screw-terminal level and the code is a short if/else loop. Prep requirement is real but reasonable — the instructor should build one working reference robot in advance and pre-test motor polarity and sensor thresholds.

ai_assistance_value.notes: Strong fit for the pipeline. Claude can author the sketch in scaffolded stages (motor test, sensor read/serial print, threshold calibration, full follow loop), wiring diagrams described step-by-step, debugging flowcharts, calibration worksheets, and extension challenges (speed tuning, handling sharp turns, line gaps).

time_scope_fit.notes: Number of sessions is not stated — only that each session is 45 minutes. A full line-following robot (assembly + wiring + motor test + sensor calibration + control logic + testing) cannot be completed in one 45-minute block by middle schoolers; realistically 3-5 sessions of 45 minutes, or 1-2 sessions if robots are pre-assembled and students only write/tune the code.

safety.notes: Low risk at 5V/battery-powered DC with no heat or chemicals. Standard mitigations to specify in the course: solderless construction only (no soldering iron with this age band), use AA/NiMH or a USB power bank rather than bare LiPo cells, supervise any use of wire strippers or hobby knives for track prep, and warn about short circuits and reversed battery polarity.

pedagogical_alignment.notes: Excellent room for productive struggle: students must choose sensor placement, determine threshold values empirically for their own room lighting, and tune turn/speed behavior. Course track design and iterative test-and-fix loops give clear decision points rather than a fixed recipe.

open_questions: How many 45-minute sessions is this unit allotted (single session, or a multi-week block of 3-5)?

What exactly is in the Arduino kits you own — specifically, do they include a chassis, DC gear motors and wheels, a motor driver/shield (L298N, TB6612, or motor shield), and IR reflectance sensors? Please list the kit brand/model if possible.
How many kits are available, and what is the expected number of students and team size (students per robot)?
Is there any budget to purchase missing parts (IR sensor modules and motor drivers are roughly $2-8 each), and what is the lead time before the club starts?
Are robot chassis pre-assembled between sessions or must students break down and rebuild each week (affects how much build time each session loses)?
suggested_changes: Confirm or scope the unit as a 3-5 session arc (e.g. S1: chassis assembly + motor test; S2: IR sensor reading and calibration; S3: control logic; S4: tuning and a timed course challenge) rather than a single 45-minute session.

If only one or two sessions are available, narrow the scope: pre-assemble and pre-wire the robots so students focus entirely on reading sensor values, setting thresholds, and writing/tuning the follow logic.
Inventory the existing kits against a parts checklist and order the likely gaps (IR reflectance sensors, motor driver boards, chassis + gear motors + battery holders) before authoring begins.
Specify solderless construction and non-LiPo power (AA pack or USB power bank) in the course requirements so the safety mitigation is baked in.
Plan the track material (black electrical tape on white poster board or vinyl) and pre-cut it, since track prep can consume a whole 45-minute block.
